approachQuestion.prompt: A rectangular board has R rows and C columns. Each cell is either open (0) or blocked (1). Starting at the top-left cell, reach the bottom-right using only one-cell moves right or down, never entering a blocked cell. Return the number of distinct move sequences modulo 1000000007. A blocked endpoint gives zero. Examples: [[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]] → 2; [[0]] → 1; [[1,0]] → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ R,C ≤ 1000. The board is rectangular and read-only.
Count the empty move sequence on a single open cell as one route. Only the modular count is returned.

options.text: Allocate C counters initialized to zero and seed counter[0]=1. Scan rows top to bottom, columns left to right. At a blocked cell reset its counter to zero; otherwise add the left counter, when present, to the existing counter, reducing modulo the modulus.
options.feedback: Before the update, the counter at this column holds routes from above and the updated counter to its left holds routes from the left. Resetting blocked cells prevents routes from passing through them; the seed also handles the single open cell.

options.text: Store a count for every cell, using zero for blocked cells, one for an open starting cell, and the sum of the counts above and left elsewhere.
options.feedback: This counts all legal routes, but rows older than the preceding row are never needed again. Keeping every cell count adds removable storage when only the final count is returned.

options.text: Return the number of ways to arrange R−1 down moves and C−1 right moves, without inspecting blocked cells.
options.feedback: Blocked cells invalidate some move sequences. For [[0,1],[0,0]], only down then right is legal, while this method counts two.

options.text: Mark open cells reachable from the start, then return 1 if the destination is reachable and 0 otherwise.
options.feedback: Reachability loses multiplicity: an entirely open two-by-two board has two distinct routes but this returns one.

feedback.reason: Initialize a counting state with one empty route and erase it at blocked cells while combining disjoint final moves.
details: Use one counter per column. Seed the first counter with one. While scanning left to right in each row, a blocked cell clears its counter; an open cell adds its left neighbor to its old counter from above, modulo 1000000007.

Before updating a column, its old counter is the route count from above; the updated previous column supplies routes from the left. A blocked cell must reset its counter to zero, not preserve last row's paths.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze rolling-board-count exactly as described: allocate and zero C counters, seed the first, and visit all R×C cells without early exits. Let R and C vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.

feedback.reason: Process RC cells using one C-counter row.
details: All RC cells are processed with constant work, including blocked cells. Initialization costs C operations and is dominated by RC because R is positive. Exactly C counters are allocated; no previous rows, routes, or stack frames are retained.
“O(R+C) time, O(C) auxiliary space”: The scan visits every cell, rather than just one row and one column.
“O(RC) time, O(RC) auxiliary space”: The fixed method overwrites one row of counters; it does not allocate a board-sized table.
“O(RC) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The C allocated counters grow with the number of columns.
